title: Tree traversals
summary: Pre-order, in-order, post-order and level order: four ways to visit every node.

steps.title: Depth-first: where does the node go?
body: To visit every node you recurse into both children. The only question is **when** you handle the node itself:
Watch `order` fill in the trace. Moving the `order.Add` line above or below the recursive calls is all that changes between the three.

code: var root = new TreeNode(4, new TreeNode(2, new TreeNode(1), new TreeNode(3)), new TreeNode(6, null, new TreeNode(7)));
public TreeNode(int value, TreeNode? left = null, TreeNode? right = null) { Value = value; Left = left; Right = right; }

steps.prompt: A **post-order** traversal of a different tree. What does it print?
code: var root = new TreeNode(5, new TreeNode(3, new TreeNode(1)), new TreeNode(8, new TreeNode(7), new TreeNode(9)));
public TreeNode(int value, TreeNode? left = null, TreeNode? right = null) { Value = value; Left = left; Right = right; }
steps.explain: Post-order finishes both children before the node, so the root comes **last**. That is the order to delete a folder tree: contents before the folder.

steps.prompt: Match each traversal to a job it suits.
pairs: copying a tree: create a node before its children
listing a binary search tree in sorted order
deleting a folder: children before the parent
printing a tree row by row

steps.title: Breadth-first: level by level
body: **Level order** visits the root, then all nodes one step down, then two steps down, and so on. Recursion naturally goes deep, so instead use a **queue**:
2. repeatedly dequeue a node, visit it, and enqueue its children.
Children join the back of the queue, so a whole level is handled before the next one starts. Watch the queue in the trace.

code: var root = new TreeNode(4, new TreeNode(2, new TreeNode(1), new TreeNode(3)), new TreeNode(6, null, new TreeNode(7)));
public TreeNode(int value, TreeNode? left = null, TreeNode? right = null) { Value = value; Left = left; Right = right; }

steps.prompt: Level order on the tree from the post-order question. What does it print?
code: var root = new TreeNode(5, new TreeNode(3, new TreeNode(1)), new TreeNode(8, new TreeNode(7), new TreeNode(9)));
public TreeNode(int value, TreeNode? left = null, TreeNode? right = null) { Value = value; Left = left; Right = right; }
steps.explain: Row 1 is 5, row 2 is 3 and 8, row 3 is 1, 7 and 9.
Dequeue first; when you record the value does not matter, but the left child must be enqueued before the right to keep each row left to right.

steps.prompt: Which traversal of a binary tree would you use with a `Stack` instead of a queue to avoid recursion?
options: A depth-first one, such as pre-order
steps.explain: Recursion uses the call stack; an explicit `Stack<TreeNode>` does the same job. Swapping the queue in level order for a stack (pushing right before left) gives pre-order.

steps.title: Three depth-first traversals
prompt: The tests provide `TreeNode` (`Value`, `Left`, `Right`). Write three functions that return the values in order:
A neat pattern: create the list, then call a recursive local function that adds to it.
solution: void Visit(TreeNode? n) { if (n == null) return; result.Add(n.Value); Visit(n.Left); Visit(n.Right); }
void Visit(TreeNode? n) { if (n == null) return; Visit(n.Left); result.Add(n.Value); Visit(n.Right); }
void Visit(TreeNode? n) { if (n == null) return; Visit(n.Left); Visit(n.Right); result.Add(n.Value); }
template: var dojoT = new TreeNode(4, new TreeNode(2, new TreeNode(1), new TreeNode(3)), new TreeNode(6, null, new TreeNode(7)));
var dojoU = new TreeNode(5, new TreeNode(3, new TreeNode(1)), new TreeNode(8, new TreeNode(7), new TreeNode(9)));
Dojo.Eq("PreOrder of a second tree", new List<int> { 5, 3, 1, 8, 7, 9 }, PreOrder(dojoU));
Dojo.Eq("PostOrder of a second tree", new List<int> { 1, 3, 7, 9, 8, 5 }, PostOrder(dojoU));
public TreeNode(int value, TreeNode? left = null, TreeNode? right = null) { Value = value; Left = left; Right = right; }
hints: Inside each function: `void Visit(TreeNode? n) { if (n == null) return; ... }`, then call `Visit(root)`.
The three differ only in where `result.Add(n.Value)` sits relative to `Visit(n.Left)` and `Visit(n.Right)`.

steps.title: Rows of a tree
prompt: Write `List<List<int>> Levels(TreeNode? root)`: the values row by row, each row left to right.
Use a queue. Trick: at the start of each row, `queue.Count` is exactly how many nodes the row has; dequeue that many and collect them.
solution: for (int i = 0, n = queue.Count; i < n; i++)
template: string DojoShow(List<List<int>> rows) => string.Join(" | ", rows.Select(r => string.Join(",", r)));
var dojoT = new TreeNode(4, new TreeNode(2, new TreeNode(1), new TreeNode(3)), new TreeNode(6, null, new TreeNode(7)));
Dojo.Eq("empty tree has no rows", "", DojoShow(Levels(null)));
var dojoChain = new TreeNode(1, null, new TreeNode(2, new TreeNode(3)));
